Recent work supports separating immediate selection from broader perceived relevance. [SM-RS 2.0 (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3754459) records choices for immediate consumption alongside explicit assessments of relevance, novelty, diversity and satisfaction; these are distinct outcomes. [In-context Ranking Preference Optimization (2025)](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=L2NPhLAKEd) addresses sparse feedback identifying relevant items rather than requiring exhaustive pairwise comparisons. Neither establishes the proposed four-way taxonomy as a validated standard.

A practical synthesis: record **choose now**, **relevant but deferred**, **explicit mismatch**, and **cannot judge/identify** separately. For pairs, ask which item better satisfies a specific evidenced need, allowing equal suitability, neither suitable, and insufficient information. Keep broad resemblance separate from a concrete match; attach the supporting title/description excerpt or history evidence to each reason. Distinguish redundancy from incompatibility, and require explicit evidence for ownership or compatibility claims. Missing specifications remain unknown. A [2025 submission’s user study](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=3ZDMQGQgkE) explicitly separates preference accuracy, target-item relevance and insufficient information, including missing titles/descriptions; its review-derived inputs exceed this task’s available evidence.

For twenty training users, report category-level counts, users contributing, judgments attempted, assessable judgments and abstentions; give uncertainty intervals and preserve repeated judgments within users when estimating uncertainty. Treat findings as exploratory failure analysis, not population preferences or validation labels. [2026 research on heterogeneous pairwise preferences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10795) shows that even many single comparisons can fail to identify population-average utility, reinforcing the need to avoid interpreting sparse pairwise wins as general preference estimates.
